entry.title: AGI is the path to freedom from intellectual labor

link.title: AGI is the path to freedom from intellectual labor

entry.content:
Most people hope that technology will free us from work. We welcome machines that lift heavy objects, software that handles repetitive paperwork, and tools that make difficult tasks easier. Yet when the work in question is intellectual, the hope often changes into fear. We want less drudgery, but we are uneasy about machines that can think and use tools.

That unease is understandable. Our jobs are not just sources of income; they give us a sense of being useful. If AI can do the work that once made us valuable, what happens to us?

But these are reasons to take the transition seriously, not reasons to pretend we want intellectual labor to remain necessary. If a system could help anyone learn, reason, design, diagnose, write, or solve problems at a level that once required years of specialized training, that would be an extraordinary expansion of human capability. AI serves to make expertise less scarce—and to let people spend less of their lives doing work simply because no one else can do it.

That is why, if we genuinely want liberation from intellectual labor, we should be rooting for AGI. AGI is not liberation by itself. It is a possibility: that the ability to think, create, and solve problems could become abundant enough to change what society asks of people. We should root for realizing that possibility, while insisting that its benefits serve humanity broadly and that the transition is worthy of the people living through it.

entry.title: Special relativity of superintelligence
entry.content:
Human intelligence’s impact grew as people preserved and combined knowledge through language, teaching, writing, institutions, and technology. Tools extended what people could do, and shared knowledge let later generations improve them. Intelligence and tools formed a snowball—not because brains evolved faster, but because ideas became cumulative and connected.

In fact, we may have become less intelligent over the past few decades because of our growing reliance on powerful tools.

AI may follow a similar trajectory on a different clock. Digital models can be copied, tested, and run in parallel. If AI helps improve software, research, or hardware, it may accelerate its next iteration. Cycles that take generations for humans could happen faster digitally.

The bold claim is that the rapid progress of superintelligence is an illusion. Rather, the “brain” of SI was born in 2022 and reached adolescence around 2025. It hasn’t become much more intelligent since then, but its ability to leverage external tools and controls has snowballed.
entry.summary: Human intelligence didn't evolve like a big bang but more like a snowball. Superintelligence is no exception.

entry.title: Training an agent that outgrows you is a false proposition

link.title: Training an agent that outgrows you is a false proposition

entry.content:
What is it like to train an agent? In the beginning it feels familiar: we provide data, set goals, give feedback, and correct mistakes. But if the aim is an agent that becomes ever more powerful, and eventually more intelligent than we are, the word “training” starts to lose its meaning.

The first analogy is the piano teacher. A good teacher can take a student a long way, but only up to what the teacher can hear. Once the student plays beyond that, the teacher can no longer tell a brilliant interpretation from a mistake. The lessons turn into encouragement, and then into listening.

A second analogy is the child and the parent. Raising a child is training of a sort, yet we do not expect to remain the authority forever. We hope some values stick, but a grown child who surpasses us makes their own judgments. Nobody calls that a failure of parenting; it is simply the point where parenting stops being the leading force.

A third analogy is the chess engine. Once engines passed the best players, humans stopped teaching them chess. The engines learn by self-play, and the humans study the engines. The direction of instruction flipped.

Training needs three things: a goal we can state, feedback we can judge, and a trainer who knows more than the trainee (agruable, but at least if the trainer is more in charge than the trainee). For a stronger agent, the second and third quietly fail. We cannot evaluate what we cannot understand, and we cannot correct what we cannot see is wrong. What remains of our role is closer to choosing what to ask, or deciding whether to trust, than to training.

These analogies are, again, incomplete. A student is not a system we build and deploy, and a child is not something we can copy a million times. Perhaps the honest description is that we are no longer training the agent past some point; we are merely the starting conditions of something that trains itself. What that means for us is a harder question than how to train it.
entry.summary: A few sloppy analogies for why "training" stops making sense once the agent is smarter than the trainer

entry.title: AI in mathematics may be less like a calculator and more like a tractor

link.title: AI in mathematics may be less like a calculator and more like a tractor

entry.content:
What is happening to mathematics as AI gets better? Perhaps it helps to compare this moment with earlier changes in how people work and how things get done.

The first analogy is mechanized agriculture. A tractor can do the work of many people, but it still takes people to operate. For a while, a small number of farmers will steer machines far stronger and more tireless than any person. AI may play a similar role in mathematics. Over time, more of the steering may be automated too, and an entire profession is gone!

A second analogy is the telescope. It did not replace astronomers; it changed what they could see. AI may become a kind of intellectual telescope for mathematics, bringing distant connections or unexpected conjectures into view. A mathematician’s job then includes deciding which glimpses are real, which are artifacts, and which deserve a closer look.

A third analogy is the computer. Computers did not make mathematics disappear; they made different mathematics possible. AI could push that boundary further, not only carrying out calculations but proposing approaches and assembling proofs.

These analogies are incomplete and, emphatically, far-cries given that AI is poised to completely take over. A tractor does not invent its own goals, a telescope does not suggest what it sees, and a traditional computer does not usually choose its own strategy. AI can do all of these things, which is why this transition feels different.
entry.summary: A few sloppy analogies for how AI is doing to mathematics

entry.title: What should students learn in the AI era?

link.title: What should students learn in the AI era?

entry.content:
The question of education in the AI era is not how schools can teach in fae of AI, but what students need to learn.

Schools and students share a common goal: helping every individual reach their full potential.

How can we do that in the AI era?

Perhaps we should start by asking the students.

entry.title: When AI is a better prover, perhaps our most important job is deciding what is worth proving.

link.title: When AI is a better prover, perhaps our most important job is deciding what is worth proving.

entry.content:
It appears any theoretical domain will be dominated by AI, including theoretical physics, if not already. Those that will fall sooner are the domains with self-contained verifications done by computation rather than experimentation.

Maybe that is where our work moves next: creating questions for AI to solve.

The important questions may not be sitting in the training data, presumably challenging for modern AI.

But perhaps “not in the training data” is not enough to make a question beyond AI.

In a world where answers are monopolized by AI, can we still be the one defining questions?

entry.title: The AI Safety Paradox
entry.content:
The argument goes like this: if we expect AI to become super-humanly intelligent, then we should pour all our efforts into making AI as capable as possible. Once it is smart enough, it will solve all our problems, including the problem of AI safety itself.

At first glance, this has a seductive internal logic. It is the ultimate delegation: build the thing that can build the solution to the thing’s own risks.

But there are several reasons this reasoning is dangerous.

First, the capability-safety gap is not guaranteed to close automatically. There is no law of physics saying that a system smart enough to solve alignment will choose to solve alignment, or that the path to superintelligence necessarily passes through a “solve alignment first” checkpoint. Capability and alignment are orthogonal dimensions—you can be arbitrarily capable while being catastrophically misaligned. (Does this make enough sense? Maybe there actually is a way…)

Second, the “AI solves AI safety” argument assumes the AI is already aligned enough to want to solve AI safety. If it is not, it has no incentive to work on the problem. This is circular: we need aligned AI to get aligned AI.

Third, irreversibility. If we bet everything on “the AI will figure it out” and we are wrong, there is no undo button. The stakes are existential; the cost of a false positive (working on safety unnecessarily) is tiny compared to the cost of a false negative (not working on safety when it was needed).

The paradox only makes sense if you assume the conclusion you are trying to prove.

(Most contents are drafted by AI, largely as my own brain food)
entry.summary: If AI is (expected to be) super-humanly intelligent, should we just build it and let it solve safety?

entry.title: Double descent, grokking, enlightenment, wisdom, aging, …

link.title: Double descent, grokking, enlightenment, wisdom, aging, …

entry.content:
In the arena of deep learning, double descent or grokking seems to insinuate a moment of sudden realization, a glimpse of wisdom sublimed from tiredless learning, and a hope of enlightenment at last.

The learning dynamics of artificial neural networks (ANN) is necessarily distinct from that of human learning.

However, the workings of ANNs may more resemble that of our human brain, particulary at the physiological level.

  1. In the early training phase, ANNs simply absorbs information via rote memorization, just like a newborn doesn’t really “know” anything but can memorize.

  2. As training goes on, sole reliance on memorization amounts to a crisis for ANNs, which are approaching its memory capacity and constantly battling confusion and conflicts caused by entanglements and correlations. This perhaps resembles the chaos in human brains at the time of puberty to maturity, too many things going on and unable to make sense of anything.

This also marks the end of the first descent phase, which is exemplified by superior learning/memorization ability and excellent performances in tasks demaining shear computing power or memorization.

  1. The second descent phase is signified by sprinkles of eureka moments, knowledge distillation for comprehension (and release of brain capacity), and enhanced reasoning ability. All these attributes are desired for model generalization on unseen samples. However, it may be accompanied by loss of memorization ability, degradation of learning capacity, and worse performances on seen samples.

Nonetheless, given a finite training set, this resolves the confusion and conflicts arising at the end of the first descent phase, leading to the second descent phase. Isn’t this how human gains wisdom?

Overall, we attempt to make an analogy between the training process of ANNs and the aging process of human brains.
entry.summary: Is there a universal rule to explain them all?

entry.title: Structure of Intelligence
entry.content:
Human intelligence rests on a collective network of neuron cells. Crucially, all neuron cells share the same underlying sets of genes and the same rules of gene regulation. The differeces between the cells, i.e., what amounts to the specialization of each cell, are the different moods/modes of functional configuration they are in. In other words, human intelligence appears to be the result of superposition, specifically, by superposing the sets of rather limited functions/genes (20K genes vs. ~12K embedding size in GPT-3) in a structured way.

What is the structure then, if any? I speculate that, the structure of human genome may offer some insights. It is the complicated, extreme “overhead” of regulatoion of the genes, only 1-2% of human genome, that makes up the bulk of genome and actually gives rise to the “cognitive behaviors” we perceive as intelligence.
entry.summary: Does the structure of articifical intelligence resemble that of human intelligence?
